conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted for abdominal pain. Can you tell me about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. It’s that same pain in my upper belly—epigastric, constant. Feels like my usual flare from pancreatitis. Not worse than before, but it’s not going away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any nausea? Vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nauseous, yes. But no vomiting. I haven’t eaten much—only a little yesterday afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And you’re not taking your Dilaudid at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not much. I try to avoid it unless it’s really bad. I don’t want to get too dependent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But uncontrolled pain can make things worse. We’ll help manage it safely. For now, we’re keeping you NPO—nothing by mouth—for a few hours to rest your pancreas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I’m used to it. But I’m worried—could this be another pancreatitis flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your lipase was elevated at 182 when you arrived—above normal. That supports acute on chronic pancreatitis, likely due to your sphincter of Oddi dysfunction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same as last time. After the ERCP, it got better. But now it’s back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we know this is recurrent. We’ll treat it supportively—IV fluids, pain control, and anti-nausea meds. Once you’re stable, we’ll slowly restart your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Thank you. I just want to feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your repeat lipase dropped to 86 this morning—trending down. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right? Does that mean it’s improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It suggests the inflammation is calming. We’re going to start you on clear liquids—water, broth, apple juice—if you can keep that down, we’ll advance to soft foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready to try. The nausea is better since the Compazine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No vomiting, and your pain is down to a 3 out of 10. We’re switching your pain meds from IV to oral Dilaudid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I prefer pills if they work. Can I go back to my regular dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve kept your home medications the same. You’ll continue 2 mg every 4 hours as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my senna and Colace? I haven’t had a bowel movement in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added scheduled senna and docusate. Constipation is common with pain meds. We’ll also give Miralax and milk of magnesia tomorrow if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I refused the enema last time. But I’ll try the oral ones.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. We’ll avoid enemas unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood pressure dropped yesterday morning to 82 over 46.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt dizzy. But I didn’t think it was serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was likely due to low fluid intake and pain. We gave you a liter of IV fluid, and your BP came up to 102 over 76. No repeat episodes since. You’re now stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s better. Should I drink more at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stay well-hydrated. And take your pain meds as prescribed—don’t let pain get severe before treating it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been tolerating a full diet—great job. No nausea or pain with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had toast, eggs, and soup. Felt okay. I’m so relieved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This is a big step. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re on track for discharge soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, can I ask about my EKG? I saw it was done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it showed sinus rhythm. A bit of delayed R wave progression and low voltage—similar to your last one. Nothing concerning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I get anxious about heart stuff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll keep an eye on it, but this isn’t new or dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look good. White count is normal, kidney function is fine. Lipase was 122 yesterday—still down from admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The acute episode is resolving. You still have chronic pancreatitis, but the flare is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave Miralax and milk of magnesia yesterday. You haven’t passed stool yet, but your belly is soft. No need to worry yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll go when I’m ready. At home, I sometimes take double the senna dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please don’t. Stick to your prescribed dose—8.6 mg twice daily. Double could cause cramping or diarrhea. If no bowel movement in 24 hours at home, call your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing so well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news! What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your regular meds, including Dilaudid as needed. Stay on clear or soft foods for a day or two. Avoid heavy, fatty meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my GI follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with Dr. ___ in one week. They’ll monitor your sphincter of Oddi dysfunction and see if further intervention is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll make sure to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your exam is stable—soft belly, no distress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take your meds, stay hydrated, eat lightly, and call your doctor if pain returns or you can’t keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I don’t have a bowel movement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nothing in 24 hours, contact your PCP. But don’t double your senna.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my anxiety—sometimes flares make me panic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your clonazepam as prescribed. And reach out to your mental health provider if you’re struggling. PTSD and chronic pain are hard to manage together.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’re here to help. A nurse will go over your discharge papers, and you can leave once ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I just want to go home and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve earned it. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.
